title: Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning - CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning - Financial Considerations
subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: What is the primary organizational benefit of implementing a well-controlled Procurement Card (P-Card) program for low-dollar, routine purchases?
options: It bypasses all budgetary constraints and funding approvals.
It allows employees to purchase personal items with post-tax payroll deductions.
It drastically reduces the high administrative costs associated with issuing traditional purchase orders and processing individual vendor invoices.
It entirely eliminates the need for formal public bidding on construction projects.
questions.explain: The main advantage of a P-Card program is efficiency. By consolidating hundreds of small purchases into one monthly electronic payment to the bank, the agency saves significant administrative overhead on requisitioning, PO generation, and invoice processing.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A buyer is executing a purchase using federal grant funds subject to 2 CFR 200 (Uniform Guidance). A key financial and legal requirement when passing federal funds to a contractor is ensuring:
options: The contract is paid in advance of the work being performed.
The inclusion of mandatory 'flow-down' clauses so the contractor must also comply with federal socio-economic and record-keeping regulations.
The contractor guarantees a 15% profit margin.
The use of an exclusively local vendor preference.
questions.explain: When utilizing federal grants, the purchasing agency must ensure that the specific legal and regulatory requirements tied to those funds 'flow down' to the contractors and subcontractors via required contract clauses (e.g., Davis-Bacon, EEO, Debarment).
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: In public sector financial management, an 'Encumbrance' is created when a Purchase Order is issued. What is the functional purpose of an encumbrance?
options: To pay the vendor immediately upon receipt of the order.
To set aside and reserve funds in the budget so they cannot be accidentally spent on another purchase before the invoice arrives.
To legally dissolve a contract if the budget is cut.
To penalize a vendor for late delivery.
questions.explain: An encumbrance is an accounting method used to reserve a portion of the budget for a specific, committed obligation (like an issued PO). It ensures that the funds will be available when the invoice is eventually received and prevents overspending.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: In large public works construction contracts, a financial mechanism is often used where the agency withholds a percentage (e.g., 5% to 10%) of each progress payment. What is this called, and what is its purpose?
options: Liquidated Damages; used to punish the contractor for early completion.
Retainage; used to provide financial leverage to ensure the contractor fully completes the project and resolves all punch-list items.
Advance Payment; used to help the contractor buy initial materials.
A Bid Bond; used to ensure the vendor honors their initial pricing.
questions.explain: Retainage is the withholding of a portion of earned payments to a contractor. It serves as an economic incentive, ensuring the contractor completes the final, often difficult, stages of a project, including defect corrections.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A vendor insists on being paid 100% of the contract price upfront before they begin providing customized software services. In public procurement, advance payments are generally:
options: Prohibited or highly restricted, as they place public funds at severe risk before value is received, and often violate constitutional prohibitions against gifting public funds.
Encouraged, as they secure better pricing from vendors.
Standard practice for all IT contracts over $1 million.
Required by federal law to support small businesses.
questions.explain: Advance payments represent a significant risk. If the vendor goes bankrupt or fails to perform, the taxpayers have lost money without receiving the service. Many state and local laws strictly forbid paying for services before they are rendered.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: To effectively control and mitigate the risk of fraud or misuse within a P-Card program, a procurement administrator should utilize:
options: An open limit with no transaction cap.
Merchant Category Code (MCC) blocking to prevent purchases at unapproved vendor types (e.g., casinos, liquor stores).
A policy allowing employees to share their physical cards with coworkers.
A system that automatically approves all transactions without manager review.
questions.explain: MCC blocking is a critical internal control in P-Card administration. It stops transactions at the point of sale if the merchant's business category is restricted by the agency's policy.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: An agency policy requires competitive bidding for purchases over $5,000. An employee has a P-Card with a single-transaction limit of $3,000. The employee needs $7,000 worth of computer monitors and tells the vendor to run the card three times on the same day for $2,333 each. This is an example of:
options: Efficient inventory management.
An unauthorized split purchase intended to circumvent procurement thresholds.
Standard demand aggregation.
A progressive payment schedule.
questions.explain: A split purchase occurs when a single requirement is artificially divided into multiple smaller transactions specifically to bypass formal competitive bidding thresholds or P-Card spending limits. This is a severe compliance violation.

questions.q: A vendor submits an invoice with the payment terms '2/10 Net 30'. How should the agency interpret this?
options: The agency will be charged a 2% penalty if they take 30 days to pay.
The invoice is due in 30 days, but the agency may take a 2% discount off the total amount if they pay within 10 days.
The agency must pay 2% of the total within 10 days, and the remaining 98% in 30 days.
The contract is only valid for 30 days.
questions.explain: '2/10 Net 30' is a standard trade credit term offering a prompt payment discount. It encourages buyers to pay invoices early (within 10 days) in exchange for a 2% reduction in price; otherwise, the full (net) amount is due in 30 days.

questions.q: A municipality separates its budget into two distinct types. The purchase of office supplies, salaries, and daily maintenance services should be funded from the:
options: Capital budget
Operating budget
Bond debt service fund
Capital improvement plan
questions.explain: An Operating budget covers the day-to-day, recurring expenses of running the government, such as salaries, utilities, and consumable supplies. The Capital budget is reserved for large, long-term investments like infrastructure and major equipment.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: During the budgeting phase, department heads are told they cannot base their requests on the previous year's budget. Instead, they must completely justify every requested expenditure starting from nothing. This methodology is known as:
options: Incremental Budgeting
Zero-Based Budgeting
Performance Budgeting
Deficit Spending
questions.explain: Zero-Based Budgeting (ZBB) requires all expenses to be justified for each new period. Unlike incremental budgeting, where the previous year's budget is adjusted by a small percentage, ZBB starts from a 'zero base'.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: The legislative body of a local government formally enacts a law or ordinance that legally authorizes the expenditure of funds for specific purposes. This legislative act is called an:
options: Encumbrance
Appropriation
Amortization
Allocation
questions.explain: An appropriation is a formal, legal authorization granted by a legislative body (like a city council or state legislature) to incur obligations and spend public funds for defined purposes during a specific period.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A procurement professional signs a multi-year IT contract that obligates $5 million total, but the legislature has only appropriated $1 million for the current fiscal year. To avoid violating 'Anti-Deficiency' laws, what clause MUST be included in the contract?
options: A Non-Appropriation (or Funding Out) clause, allowing the agency to cancel the contract without penalty if future funds are not appropriated.
An advance payment clause to get all the money upfront.
A liquidated damages clause against the state legislature.
A Cost-Plus-Percentage-of-Cost clause.
questions.explain: Anti-deficiency statutes prohibit agencies from obligating the government to pay more money than is legally appropriated. A Non-Appropriation clause protects the agency by terminating the contract if subsequent funding is denied by the legislative body.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Under what circumstance does the 'Release of Retainage' generally occur in a public construction project?
options: When the project is 50% complete.
Upon 'Substantial Completion' or Final Acceptance of the project, meaning the facility is ready for its intended use and punch list items are resolved.
Prior to the Notice to Proceed being issued.
At the beginning of each fiscal year.
questions.explain: Retainage is held until the end of the project. It is typically released to the contractor only after the architect or project manager certifies 'Substantial Completion' and ensures that all defects (punch list items) have been satisfactorily corrected.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A local government receives a specialized federal grant to hire more police officers. The terms explicitly state that grant funds must be used to INCREASE the total number of officers, not to pay for the existing ones. Using the funds for existing officers violates the rule against:
options: Supplementing
Supplanting
Amortizing
Capitalizing
questions.explain: Federal grants typically carry 'supplement, not supplant' provisions. This means federal funds must be used to add to (supplement) existing state/local funds, not replace (supplant) local funds that were already budgeted for the same purpose.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Any non-federal entity that expends $750,000 or more in federal awards during its fiscal year is legally required to undergo a specialized, rigorous financial review known as a:
options: Single Audit (under the Single Audit Act).
Value Analysis Audit.
Reverse Auction Audit.
Quality Assurance Inspection.
questions.explain: Under 2 CFR 200 (Subpart F), state, local, and non-profit entities spending $750,000 or more in federal grant funds annually must undergo a 'Single Audit' to ensure compliance with federal program requirements.
